subject: Cognitive Science
title: Illusory Correlations
description: A fast breakdown of Illusory Correlations for builders.

hook.text: A tourist gets robbed in a city and forever calls it dangerous. One event, permanent category.

buildup.text: Illusory correlation is seeing a link between two things that aren't actually related.

discovery.text: Hamilton and Gifford showed that rare events in rare groups get mentally overlinked and remembered.

twist.text: Distinctive pairings stand out in memory, so small groups get blamed for unusual behaviors.

climax.text: This basic memory glitch feeds real-world prejudice without any malicious intent needed.

punchline.text: Rare plus rare feels like a pattern.

quiz.question: What causes illusory correlations?
options: Distinctive pairings are easier to remember
Large sample sizes cause the error

details.summary: Illusory correlations are perceived relationships between events that are not actually related. People overestimate the link between distinctive events and distinctive groups, which can fuel stereotypes. The bias exists because unusual combinations are more memorable and mentally available.
details.whyItMatters: Illusory correlations explain how stereotypes form even in the absence of real statistical associations. Awareness of this bias is a first step toward correcting it.
takeaways: People perceive correlations that do not exist in the data
Distinctive event pairs are overrepresented in memory
This bias contributes to stereotype formation and maintenance

faq.question: How do illusory correlations create stereotypes?
faq.answer: If a minority group member does something negative, both the person and the act are distinctive. This double distinctiveness makes the event highly memorable, inflating the perceived association between the group and the behavior. The same behavior by a majority member goes unnoticed.

faq.question: Can illusory correlations be corrected?
faq.answer: Awareness helps but does not eliminate them. Providing base rate information and encouraging statistical thinking reduces the bias. Intergroup contact also helps by providing counter-examples that weaken the perceived association between groups and negative behaviors.
